name: The Authorship Rule
title: The Authorship Rule
answer: The Authorship Rule is a clear school-wide agreement that students must make their own creative work and disclose any AI help they use. It matters because without it a student can submit AI-generated art believing nothing is wrong, and with it everyone knows where the line sits.

crumbs.name: Arts, Music, Physical Education, and Health

sections.body: The Authorship Rule sets a single, simple expectation for creative subjects: the student makes the work, and any AI assistance is disclosed. It solves the confusion that arises when schools have no shared position, where a student might hand in an image generated in seconds for an art assignment and genuinely think that is acceptable. The rule does not ban AI outright. It names the specific, limited ways AI may support creative work, such as brainstorming ideas for a painting, finding reference images, or learning about an artist's techniques. What it forbids is presenting work made by AI as the student's own creation.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In day to day teaching, the rule works as a posted and shared statement, which the book presents as Figure 10.3 in a form teachers can display and send to families. Most creative assignments sit at the lower AI use levels described in Chapter 3, meaning AI plays little or no part in the making. A small number of assignments may explore AI directly, for example a project in which a student compares their own drawing with one generated by AI and discusses the differences, and those tasks are clearly labelled as such. Students may use layout tools such as Canva for Education or Adobe Express for Education for a poster, provided the artwork and the design choices remain their own. The text does not separate this practice by grade band, though it notes that the copyright discussion suits older students.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea as practice rather than research. Its supporting material is a legal point rather than a study: UNESCO's guidance notes that the United States Copyright Office has said output generated by AI is not protected by copyright, because copyright protects only work that comes from human creativity (Miao & Holmes, 2023). The book treats that point as a discussion starter for older students, connecting the classroom rule to a real question about what makes creative work belong to someone. No classroom trial, sample or measured outcome is offered for the rule itself.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are stated plainly: AI may support thinking and layout, but it cannot be the author of the work, and any help that is used must be disclosed. Assignments that deliberately involve AI, such as comparing a student drawing with a generated one, must be clearly labelled so they are not mistaken for ordinary creative tasks. The judgement about whether a piece of work is genuinely the student's own stays with the teacher, and the decision about which assignments sit at which AI use level stays with the school. The copyright point is presented as a teaching topic, not as legal advice, and the book does not extend the rule beyond creative work.
